questions.prompt: The secant equation asks a Hessian approximation \(B\) to satisfy
options: \(B s = y\), where \(s\) is the step and \(y\) is the change in the gradient
questions.explanation: Along the step just taken, the gradient change is the action of an average Hessian. The secant equation asks \(B\) to match that action: \(B s = y\). The identity satisfies it only when \(s = y\). A zero step makes \(B s = y\) impossible unless \(y\) is zero too, and a zero step is not a useful update. Orthogonality would make \(B s\) perpendicular to \(s\), while the equation sets \(B s\) equal to \(y\).

questions.prompt: A scalar step is \(s = -1\) and the gradient change is \(y = -2\). The secant equation \(B s = y\) forces \(B\) to equal
questions.explanation: The equation is \(B \cdot (-1) = -2\), so \(B = 2\). For \(f(t) = t^2\) this is the constant second derivative: a step from \(2\) to \(1\) changes the derivative from \(4\) to \(2\). Reporting \(-2\) keeps the ratio \(y/s\) without canceling the two minus signs. Reporting \(-1\) is the step. Reporting \(1\) is the reciprocal of the absolute step.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The fundamental theorem along the segment from \(x\) to \(x+s\) says that the gradient change \(y\) equals
options: the change in the objective divided by the gradient
a matrix that is singular at every point of the segment
the integral, along the segment, of the Hessian applied to \(s\)
questions.explanation: Integrating the derivative of the gradient along the segment produces \(y = \int_0^1 \nabla^2 f(x + \tau s)\, s\, d\tau\). That is an average Hessian times \(s\). The secant equation replaces the average by a single matrix \(B\). The gradient at the old point is not the change. The objective change is a scalar and is not \(y\). The integral does not claim that every Hessian on the segment is singular.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of one secant update in order. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The change \(y\) is a difference of gradients, so both gradients come first. The secant equation names \(y\) on the right-hand side, so \(y\) has to exist before the equation can be imposed. The Newton system uses the approximation that satisfies the equation, so it comes last. Solving a system before the gradients are evaluated would use a model from the wrong point.

steps: Evaluate the gradient at the current point and at the point reached by a step \(s\).
Subtract those two gradients to form the change \(y\).
Require the new approximation to send \(s\) to \(y\).
Use that approximation in place of the Hessian in the Newton linear system.

questions.prompt: Which scalar pairs \((s, y)\) admit a positive definite approximation \(B\) with \(B s = y\)?
questions.explanation:
In one variable, \(B s = y\) with \(B > 0\) means \(s \ne 0\) and \(y/s > 0\).
• \(6/2 = 3 > 0\).
• \(-6/2 = -3 < 0\), so the only solution is negative.
• \((-2)/(-1) = 2 > 0\).
• \(B \cdot 0 = 1\) has no solution.
• \((-8)/(-4) = 2 > 0\).
The same sign test is \(y s > 0\). A negative product cannot be \(s B s\) for a positive \(B\).

questions.prompt: For a nonzero scalar step \(s\) and a gradient change \(y\), the secant value \(B\) equals
questions.explanation: The equation \(B s = y\) has one unknown. Dividing by \(s\) gives \(B = y/s\). Both declared names appear. The reciprocal \(s/y\) is the matching inverse approximation, not \(B\). The product \(y s\) is the curvature product, not the secant value. The sum \(y + s\) does not solve \(B s = y\).

questions.prompt: A note builds a Hessian approximation for \(s = (1,\ 0)\) and \(y = (2,\ 0)\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The equation \(B s = y\) with \(s = (1,\ 0)\) reads off the first column, which must be \(y = (2,\ 0)\). The second column is multiplied by the zero component of \(s\), so it is free. The diagonal matrix with \(2\)s on the diagonal is one solution, and so is every matrix whose first column is \((2,\ 0)\), including one whose second column is \((5,\ 7)\). One secant equation is \(n\) conditions on an \(n \times n\) matrix.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a diagonal array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   b</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A two-by-two array with labels on the diagonal.
steps: The secant equation asks for \(B s = y\).
The first column of \(B\) must be \((2,\ 0)\).
This one equation does not constrain the second column of \(B\).
Therefore \(B\) equals \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) and no other matrix.
reasons: One secant equation fixes only the action of \(B\) on \(s\). The second column can still change.
The secant equation does not ask for \(B s = y\).

questions.prompt: Let \(s = (2,\ 0)\) and \(y = (6,\ 0)\). What is the curvature \((y^T s) / (s^T s)\)?
questions.explanation: The products are \(y^T s = 12\) and \(s^T s = 4\), so the ratio is \(3\). That is the value a scalar secant approximation would take, and it is also \(s^T B s / s^T s\) for any \(B\) with \(B s = y\). Reporting \(12\) skips the division. Reporting \(4\) is \(s^T s\). Reporting \(2\) is the first entry of \(s\).

questions.prompt: On a quadratic whose Hessian \(H\) is constant, the secant equation is satisfied by
options: no matrix, because a constant Hessian has \(y = 0\)
the true Hessian, for every step \(s\)
questions.explanation: A constant Hessian gives \(y = H s\) for every step, by the fundamental theorem or by direct expansion. So \(H\) itself solves \(B s = y\). The identity solves it only when \(H s = s\). The gradient change is \(H s\), which is zero only when \(s\) is in the null space. An approximation that ignores \(y\) cannot enforce the equation.

questions.prompt: Among updates that enforce the secant equation and stay symmetric, the one that preserves positive definiteness when \(y^T s > 0\) is
options: a replacement of the approximation by a skew-symmetric matrix
a rule that sets \(y\) to zero after the step
questions.explanation: BFGS is a symmetric rank-two update. It satisfies \(B_+ s = y\), and if the previous matrix is positive definite and \(y^T s > 0\), the new matrix is positive definite. A skew-symmetric matrix has \(s^T B s = 0\), so it cannot represent a positive curvature product. Setting \(y\) to zero destroys the secant equation unless \(s\) is zero. Forcing \(y^T s = 0\) is the case positive definiteness cannot satisfy.

questions.prompt: A scalar approximation currently equals \(4\). The new step is \(s = 1\) and the gradient change is \(y = 2\). What is the secant residual \(y - B s\)?
questions.explanation: The current approximation predicts \(B s = 4\). The observed change is \(2\), so the residual is \(2 - 4 = -2\). An update that enforces the secant equation has to cancel this residual. Reporting \(2\) is \(y\). Reporting \(4\) is the old prediction. Reporting \(6\) adds them.

options: No positive definite matrix satisfies the secant equation \(B s = y\).
Every positive definite matrix satisfies \(B s = y\).
The gradient change \(y\) is the zero vector whenever \(s\) is not zero.
questions.explanation: If \(B\) is positive definite and \(s \ne 0\), then \(s^T B s > 0\). The secant equation would make that product equal \(s^T y\). A nonpositive \(s^T y\) is therefore impossible. It does not follow that every positive definite matrix works: the equation is a particular action on \(s\). Nor does it follow that \(s\) or \(y\) vanishes. The pair \(s = 1\), \(y = -1\) has a negative product and neither vector is zero.
